title: Microsoft disrupts AI-assisted platform that compromised 12,000 accounts
content:
Microsoft said Tuesday that it led an industry-wide disruption of a subscription-based scam platform that used an AI chatbot to compromise 12,000 Microsoft accounts over a few-month span.
Named EvilTokens, the platform was introduced over a Telegram channel in February and charged an initial $1,500 fee and a recurring $500 charge each month after that. EvilTokens provided a single service for streamlining most steps required to compromise email accounts in large numbers. From there, the platform helped customers analyze inboxes, select targets that would provide the biggest potential payouts, and draft follow-up emails that provided realistic ruses for tricking company employees into transferring funds to attacker-controlled accounts.
Minutes, not days
“While EvilTokens helped cybercriminals access email accounts, at the center of the service was an AI-style chatbot that could analyze a victim’s inbox and help criminals identify trusted relationships, payment authorizations, and sensitive responsibilities, as well as other circumstances where fraud was most likely to succeed,” Microsoft said. “The platform could even recommend fraud strategies, including drafting messages that impersonated trusted contacts to help criminals trick victims into taking action.”
Microsoft said users of EvilToken compromised 12,000 customer accounts belonging to 10,000 organizations around the world, with the highest concentration of them located in the US. Countries with the next-largest numbers were Canada, the UK, Australia, India, and France. Victim organizations included wholesale distribution, construction, financial services, real estate, higher education, and healthcare. SpyCloud, a security firm that assisted in the disruption operation, has more details about victims here.
Using a legal process and a network of partners, Microsoft seized 50 websites and 150 more domains used to operate EvilTokens. The UK’s Metropolitan Police Service arrested two men on suspicion of offenses allegedly connected to the crime platform.
Account compromises were achieved through a legitimate OAuth process known as device code authentication. This form of authentication is designed for TVs and input-constrained devices, meaning those that lack the interface for performing normal log-in processes. In this model, the device being signed into presents a code and instructs the user to enter it into a browser on a separate device. The new device is then authenticated.

report.summary: Microsoft disrupted EvilTokens, an AI chatbot-powered subscription service that compromised 12,000 Microsoft accounts across 10,000 organizations worldwide.
report.background: Phishing-as-a-service has grown into a mature criminal industry, letting low-skilled attackers rent tools instead of building them. EvilTokens fits that trend but adds an AI chatbot that automates the hardest parts: reading a victim's inbox, spotting payment approvals and trusted contacts, and writing convincing follow-up emails. The attack abused OAuth device code authentication, a legitimate flow meant for smart TVs and other input-limited devices. Attackers trick a user into entering a code on a Microsoft login page, which silently authorizes the attacker's device and grants access to email. This bypasses passwords and often multi-factor protections. Microsoft's disruption, conducted with security partners and UK police, shows cloud identity providers moving aggressively against criminal infrastructure that targets their own authentication systems.
key_points: EvilTokens launched on Telegram in February as a subscription service costing $1,500 up front plus $500 monthly. It bundled account compromise, inbox analysis, target selection, and email drafting into one platform, with an AI-style chatbot at the center that recommended fraud strategies and impersonated trusted contacts.

Microsoft says the platform compromised 12,000 customer accounts across 10,000 organizations worldwide. The US had the highest concentration, followed by Canada, the UK, Australia, India, and France. Victims spanned wholesale distribution, construction, financial services, real estate, higher education, and healthcare, sectors where business email compromise can trigger large fraudulent payments.

Attackers used device code authentication, an OAuth flow designed for TVs and input-constrained devices. The attacker's device shows a code; the victim enters it in a browser and authenticates that device. Because it is a legitimate flow, it can bypass MFA and leave security teams with few obvious red flags beyond unusual token grants.

Microsoft seized 50 websites and 150 additional domains through legal process and partner coordination. The UK Metropolitan Police arrested two men suspected of offenses linked to the platform. Security firm SpyCloud assisted and published victim details.

The chatbot compressed reconnaissance and social engineering from days to minutes, letting criminals quickly identify who approves payments and craft realistic impersonation emails. Microsoft framed the AI as the service's core, not a side feature.
report.impact: The disruption shows how quickly AI is industrializing cybercrime. Attackers no longer need phishing expertise; a chatbot can read an inbox and write convincing fraud emails. That lowers the barrier for entry and increases the volume of business email compromise. For developers and IT admins, the device code flow is a sharp reminder that legitimate OAuth features can be abused; organizations should restrict or monitor device code authentication, enforce conditional access, and deploy phishing-resistant MFA. For regular users, the lesson is never to enter a login code they did not initiate, even if it appears on a real Microsoft page. For the AI industry, the case adds pressure to prevent models from being repurposed for fraud, while Microsoft's takedown signals that cloud providers will pursue criminal infrastructure aggressively.
report.tools: Defenders can watch Microsoft Entra ID Conditional Access policies for blocking or limiting device code flow, plus phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2 security keys and passkeys. SpyCloud provides breach and credential exposure monitoring; Have I Been Pwned helps individuals check exposure. Open-source Microsoft 365 security assessment tools like Maester and 365Inspect can help admins audit tenant configurations. For threat research, Microsoft's device code phishing guidance and OAuth token monitoring resources are worth following.
